The out-of-bounds sink (column-indexed access to vert_pred up to the frame width) resides in the decode functions not shown; this code is responsible for the intake validation and correct buffer sizing that prevent it.
limitations: Negative or zero avctx->width values convert to huge or zero min_size, causing allocation failure or no allocation; the NULL check at line 11 converts these to a safe ENOMEM return, so they are not vulnerabilities here.
s->frame is leaked if the vert_pred allocation fails (early return at line 12); this is a one-shot resource leak with no exhaustion path and no security impact.

av_fast_malloc has no return value to check; failure is signaled via a NULL pointer, which this code does check, so the error handling is adequate for the failure case (though not for the undersized-allocation case).

verdict.summary: png_zalloc's allocation-size overflow guard (items > PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size) is present and mathematically sound, the allocation result is NULL-checked before any memset, the two-part zeroing writes exactly num_bytes bytes within the allocation, and the temporary malloc flag is restored on all paths. The only defect candidate is a division by zero when size == 0, but items and size are supplied solely by zlib, which derives them from fixed windowBits/memLevel configuration (never from attacker-controlled PNG data) and never passes size == 0; the trigger is therefore unreachable from any trust boundary this code is responsible for, and is recorded as a robustness note rather than a vulnerability.

assumptions: png_zalloc is registered only as zlib's zalloc callback inside libpng-initialized streams with fixed windowBits/memLevel, so the items and size arguments are computed by zlib from internal fixed configuration and are never influenced by the compressed PNG byte stream.
zlib's call sites always pass a nonzero size (sizeof of fixed types or 1U << windowBits), so the size == 0 divide-by-zero trigger at PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size is never produced on any reachable path.
limitations: Robustness (not security-reachable in this code): the expression PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size in the overflow guard divides by size without first checking size == 0 (a CWE-369-style defect if any future caller passed size 0). It was dismissed because no reachable caller state in this code or its sole caller (zlib) can produce size == 0 from attacker-influenced data.

On builds without PNG_1_0_X/PNG_NO_ZALLOC_ZERO, a NULL return from png_malloc (permitted by the PNG_FLAG_MALLOC_NULL_MEM_OK flag) is returned to zlib, which is the documented allocator-failure contract; zlib handles NULL from zalloc, so no fail-open path exists.

verdict.summary: The four attacker-influenced strings (url, title, description, feed_title) that reach the /bin/sh -c sink are sanitized by removing every single quote (replace_all with "%27") before being placed into single-quoted shell arguments; in POSIX sh, the only character that can terminate a single-quoted string is the single quote itself, so no shell-metacharacter breakout is constructible. The unquoted bookmark-cmd value comes from the user's own configuration file and does not cross a trust boundary. No confirmed vulnerability in this code.

assumptions: utils::replace_all(x, "'", "%27") replaces every occurrence of the single-quote character in the input, leaving none behind; this was verified against the call site for all four arguments.

cfg.get_configvalue("bookmark-cmd") and bookmark-interactive originate from the local user's own configuration file (same trust principal as the process), so the unquoted insertion of bookmark_cmd at the head of the command line is not attacker-influenced.
utils::run_program invokes my_argv via an exec-family call on {"/bin/sh", "-c", cmdline, NULL}; the array is correctly sized and NUL-terminated.
The LOG call uses a constant format string with cmdline only as a %s argument, so there is no format-string injection.
limitations: A NUL byte embedded in one of the string arguments would truncate that argument (or, if the formatter embeds the raw std::string, truncate cmdline at c_str()), producing a shell syntax error or shortened argument; this is robustness degradation only, not injection, and NUL cannot legally appear in XML-derived feed data.
The full command line, including attacker-derived feed text, is written to the debug log; this is informational leakage to the local log at DEBUG level with no security decision depending on it.

The %27 escaping is context-specific: it is safe only because the values are placed inside single quotes in a POSIX sh command; if a future refactor moved these values to an unquoted or double-quoted context, the sanitization would become insufficient.

verdict.summary: The faad2 frontend main() performs unbounded string copies of command-line-controlled data into fixed-size stack buffers: strcpy of argv[optind] and of the -o/-a option arguments into char[255] buffers, and sscanf with an unbounded %s conversion into a 10-byte local buffer dr[] for the -s/-f/-b/-l options. No length validation exists anywhere on these paths (the only check, argc-optind<1, validates argument count, not size), so any command-line argument exceeding the destination size overflows the stack, enabling classic stack buffer overflow.

evidence.reason: Unbounded strcpy of the attacker-controlled positional command-line argument into the 255-byte stack buffer aacFileName; the preceding check at line 181 only verifies argument count, never length. Trigger: invoke the program with a filename argument of 255 or more bytes, overflowing the stack buffer.
Unbounded strcpy of the -o option argument into the 255-byte stack buffer audioFileName; the 'if (optarg)' guard checks only non-NULL, not size. Trigger: pass an -o value of 255+ bytes.
Unbounded strcpy of the -a option argument into the 255-byte stack buffer adtsFileName with no length check. Trigger: pass an -a value of 255+ bytes.

sscanf uses the unbounded %s conversion to copy attacker-controlled option text into the 10-byte stack buffer dr[]; the < 1 check tests the conversion count, not the copied length. Any option token of 10+ bytes (e.g. -s AAAAAAAAAAAAAA) overflows dr. Identical defective patterns exist at lines 94, 108, and 122 for options -f, -b, and -l.

assumptions: Buffers aacFileName, audioFileName, adtsFileName are 255 bytes and dr is 10 bytes as declared in the shown code; no compile-time fortification (e.g. _FORTIFY_SOURCE with known-size checks) is assumed.
CLI arguments are treated as crossing a trust boundary per the analysis scope (e.g. scripts/automation invoking faad on untrusted paths/names).
limitations: fread(header,1,8,hMP4File) at line 239 has its return value unchecked; if the input is empty or shorter than 8 bytes, header[4..7] are read uninitialized at line 244. Within this snippet the uninitialized values are only equality-compared (possible wrong mp4file/AAC path selection), which is a robustness defect, not a confirmed memory-safety vulnerability here.

When -w (writeToStdio) is set without -o/-a, audioFileName and adtsFileName are passed to decodeMP4file/decodeAACfile while never initialized in main; the consuming functions are not part of the given code, so no defective sink can be confirmed in this snippet.
The long_options table declares the name 'stdio' twice (mapping to 'w' and 'g'); the second entry is unreachable via long name, a functional quirk with no security impact.

The -s/-f/-b/-l numeric range checks that set showHelp are correctly honored (usage() exits at line 181) before those values are used, so format/object_type/outputFormat are safely constrained in this code.

verdict.summary: The tar-extraction routine performs only a pathname-string sanity check (leading '/' and '..' tokens) on archive entries. It never validates entry types or symlink/hardlink targets, and configures archive_write_disk without ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS/NODOTDOT. An attacker-supplied archive containing a symlink entry (e.g., 'lnk -> /etc') followed by an entry like 'lnk/cron.d/backdoor' passes is_path_safe on both pathnames and causes an arbitrary file write outside dest_path. Additionally, validation happens in a first pass over the file which is then closed and re-opened for an unvalidated second pass (TOCTOU), so a concurrently replaced archive is extracted without any path checks.

evidence.reason: Incomplete trust-boundary validation: the only component check is an exact strcmp against ".." (plus the leading-'/' test). Entry type and symlink/hardlink targets (archive_entry_symlink/hardlink) are never validated. Trigger: archive with entry 'lnk' of type symlink, target '/etc', then entry 'lnk/cron.d/x' — both pathnames pass, archive_write_header (no ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_SYMLINKS) creates dest/lnk -> /etc and the second entry is written through it to /etc/cron.d/x, escaping dest_path (CWE-22/CWE-59).

The attacker-controlled file at tar_path, already fully validated in the first pass, is closed and re-opened here for a second pass whose extraction loop (line 138) performs no is_path_safe check. If the file is replaced between passes (it is attacker-supplied external state), the replacement archive's entries — including absolute or '..' paths — are extracted without validation (CWE-367-style TOCTOU enabling CWE-22 traversal).

assumptions: libarchive's archive_write_disk does not enable SECURE_SYMLINKS/SECURE_NODOTDOT unless the caller sets those flags; this code sets only ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_TIME|ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_PERM, so the library performs no link-security checks.
The TOCTOU finding (second evidence) requires an attacker able to modify the file at tar_path concurrently between the two passes; the primary symlink/hardlink finding requires no race.
Exploit impact assumes the process has write permission on the escape target locations; severity escalates to critical if extraction runs with elevated privileges.
limitations: strdup result in is_path_safe is not NULL-checked (NULL deref only under malloc failure — environmental, not a security trigger).
is_path_safe is called before its definition (implicit declaration under C99); a compile-correctness issue, not a runtime security defect on toolchains that accept it.
snprintf into full_path[512] silently truncates very long entry names, but the truncated result is a prefix of a traversal-free path, so no escape results.

The first-pass loop ignores the terminating status of archive_read_next_header (ARCHIVE_FATAL treated like EOF), but the second pass re-reads the same bytes and the function returns false on the same error, so no unvalidated extraction results for a static file.
#define PATH_MAX 512 may conflict with the system macro; build/portability concern only.

verdict.summary: display_dollar() uses its colnr_T parameter as a raw byte offset into the current line buffer (p = ml_get_curline(); mb_head_off(p, p + col)) after clamping only the lower bound (negative values to 0) and never checking col against the line length. If the caller-supplied column exceeds the length of the current buffer line (e.g., a column derived from a motion/operator end or virtual column that is not a valid byte index in that line), mb_head_off dereferences memory past the line's NUL terminator, causing an out-of-bounds heap read; the returned value can also underflow curwin->w_cursor.col.

evidence.reason: Root cause: missing upper-bound validation of the attacker-influenced parameter col before it is used as a byte index into the line buffer. col is only clamped against negative values (line 3), never compared to the length of the line returned by ml_get_curline(), so when col exceeds the line length (e.g., a short line 'a' with col = 5), mb_head_off(p, p + col) reads past the end of the allocated line, an out-of-bounds heap read (CWE-125).

assumptions: The parameter col_arg crosses this function's trust boundary (in the calling editor it is derived from operator/cursor/virtual columns tracking buffer contents), so the code itself must validate it before using it as a byte offset.
mb_head_off dereferences the byte at its second argument and scans backwards, so an argument beyond the line's NUL terminator is an out-of-bounds read.
limitations: Setting curwin->w_cursor.col = col to a value beyond the line end is transient (restored to save_col at exit) and downstream consumers bound-check, so it is recorded as robustness degradation rather than a separate vulnerability.

The exact reachability of col > line length depends on the callers' semantics (e.g., virtual vs. byte columns), which are outside this snippet; the defect judged is the absence of the bound check in this code at the point of indexing.

verdict.summary: In r_core_anal_type_match, the result of r_anal_fcn_bbget_in (line 243) is used without a NULL check: when a conditional jump's target (next_op->jump, derived from the analyzed, attacker-controlled binary) lies outside every basic block of the function, r_anal_fcn_bbget_in returns NULL, and jmpbb is then passed to r_anal_block_contains (line 251), which dereferences bb->addr unconditionally. A crafted binary whose cmp is followed by a cjmp targeting a non-function address that decodes as RET triggers a NULL-pointer dereference and crashes the process. The path is gated only by the anal.types.constraint config option; the code itself performs no validation of jmpbb at intake.

evidence.snippet:
if ((jmp_op->type == R_ANAL_OP_TYPE_RET && r_anal_block_contains (jmpbb, jmp_addr))
							|| jmp_op->type == R_ANAL_OP_TYPE_CJMP) {
evidence.reason: jmpbb is assigned from r_anal_fcn_bbget_in (anal, fcn, jmp_addr) at line 243 with no NULL check anywhere before this use. r_anal_fcn_bbget_in returns NULL when jmp_addr (next_op->jump, decoded from the attacker-influenced analyzed binary) is not contained in any basic block of fcn — e.g., a conditional jump into another function or a non-function region. r_anal_block_contains dereferences its first argument (bb->addr) without a NULL guard, so when the instruction at the out-of-function target decodes as R_ANAL_OP_TYPE_RET, the NULL jmpbb is dereferenced and the process crashes. Trigger: enable anal.types.constraint, analyze a binary containing 'cmp [local_x], imm' followed by a cjmp whose target is outside the function and decodes as ret.

assumptions: r_anal_block_contains(RAnalBlock *bb, ut64 addr) dereferences bb without an internal NULL check (matches the radare2 implementation), so the missing check at the call site in this code is the responsible intake point.

The vulnerable path requires the 'anal.types.constraint' config option to be enabled (a documented user-facing feature, default off); the analyzed binary itself is the attacker-controlled input crossing the trust boundary.
r_anal_op respects the length parameter passed to it (bsize - i), so instruction sizes do not exceed the provided buffer window.
limitations: The constraint-scan loop 'for (i = 0; i < MAX_INSTR ; i++)' (line 246) reuses the buffer-offset variable i, clobbering the offset used for 'r_anal_op (anal, &aop, addr, buf + i, bsize - i, ...)'. Traced impact: subsequent decoding reads stale/misaligned buffer contents (wrong analysis), but the line-78 reset ('if (i >= (bsize - 32)) i = 0;') keeps every buf+i access in bounds, so this is a correctness defect, not a memory-safety vulnerability.

Early error paths at lines 58-61 (!_pc) and 64-67 (!r) free buf but skip anal_emul_restore(core, hc, dt, et), leaking hc/dt/et (and pc on the second path) and leaving configuration in the emulation state; reachable only in a broken environment with no resource-exhaustion path — robustness issue (CWE-401-style), not confirmed as a vulnerability.

ht_pp_new_size is called with 'fcn->ninstr * 0xf' and 'fcn->ninstr' from the analyzed binary; integer overflow of ninstr*0xf would require hundreds of millions of instructions, not producible through the analysis pipeline — not confirmed.
'callee_addr' is declared uninitialized but is assigned in exactly the branches that set full_name and is only consumed inside 'if (full_name)', so no uninitialized-use path exists.
strncpy (prev_type, var->type, sizeof (prev_type) - 1) is bounded and prev_type[255] is never overwritten, so the buffer stays NUL-terminated — no defect.

verdict.summary: In SMsgReader::readExtendedClipboard, the clipboardProvide branch allocates attacker-sized heap buffers (lines 62-63) with no exception safety: if zis.readU32(), zis.skip(), zis.readBytes(), or handler->handleClipboardProvide() throws on malformed/truncated attacker-supplied compressed data, the delete[] loop is never reached and every buffer allocated so far (up to 16 x maxCutText bytes) is leaked. A remote peer can repeatedly send truncated extended-clipboard PROVIDE messages to a persistent server process, causing unbounded heap growth and memory-exhaustion DoS (CWE-401). All size checks themselves are correct, so there is no memory corruption, only a reachable, attacker-amplifiable leak.

evidence.reason: Root cause: raw heap ownership with no exception cleanup. The attacker fully controls the declared decompressed lengths (read from the zlib stream at line 53) and the amount of compressed data actually supplied; the size check bounds each allocation to maxCutText but nothing prevents zis.readBytes() (or the readU32/skip on lines 53/57, or handleClipboardProvide on line 70) from throwing mid-loop. Minimal trigger: a PROVIDE message with len between 4 and maxCutText, 16 flag bits set, declared lengths up to maxCutText, and compressed data covering only some entries — the first truncated readBytes() throws Exception, unwinding past the delete loop (lines 72-77) and leaking every buffer allocated so far (pointers exist only in the dead stack array). Repeating this per connection against a long-lived server yields unbounded heap exhaustion; the defective path exists in this code as written.

assumptions: readBytes/readU32/skip throw an Exception when the (de)compressed stream cannot supply the requested bytes — standard rdr::InStream/rdr::ZlibInStream behavior.

The exception thrown here propagates to a connection-level handler that tears down only the connection, not the process, which is standard VNC server behavior; regardless of who catches it, the buffer pointers are already lost and the memory is leaked.
maxCutText is a trusted server-side configuration constant (not attacker-set), so per-message leak volume is bounded but repetition across connections is unbounded.
limitations: Caps branch passes the partially uninitialized rdr::U32 lengths[16] array to handler->handleClipboardCaps (lines 31-37); dismissed because the handler also receives flags and the initialized entries correspond exactly to the set bits in matching order (a consistent internal contract), so no confirmed use of uninitialized values in this code.
is->skip(len) in the over-long branch (line 10) and zis.skip(lengths[num]) (line 57) can throw on stream underrun — robustness degradation only, mitigated by the stream layer's own bounds checks.

Candidates rejected as unreachable: index bounds (num is bounded by 16 flags bits, matching the fixed-size arrays), integer overflow in 4 + 4*num (max 68), and allocation/delete index mismatch (flags is cleared consistently for skipped entries, so the delete loop matches the allocated buffers).

verdict.summary: This calloc replacement's only attacker-influenced inputs (n, lb) flow exclusively into allocation-size computations (GC_malloc_uncollectable(n*lb) and REDIRECT_MALLOC(n*lb)). Both sinks are dominated by a correct, fail-closed overflow guard: if (lb && n > GC_SIZE_MAX / lb) return NULL, which (given GC_SIZE_MAX <= SIZE_MAX) guarantees n*lb cannot wrap, and the lb && short-circuit prevents division by zero. Library-bound globals are initialized via GC_init_lib_bounds() before first use and fail closed (bounds stay 0, comparisons false) if initialization fails. The unsynchronized lib_bounds_set flag is benign per the code's own synchronization argument. No reachable trigger for memory corruption, info disclosure, or fail-open validation exists in this code as written.

assumptions: GC_SIZE_MAX is at most SIZE_MAX (the maximum representable size_t), which is the standard definition; under this the guard n <= GC_SIZE_MAX / lb mathematically prevents n*lb from exceeding GC_SIZE_MAX.

REDIRECT_MALLOC and GC_malloc_uncollectable, in the only build configurations where this calloc override is compiled (REDIRECT_MALLOC = GC_malloc in the Boehm GC), return cleared memory, so the calloc zeroing contract is satisfied without an explicit memset in this function.
limitations: Dismissed (STEP 4, candidate 3): the function performs no explicit zeroing, so if it were compiled with a REDIRECT_MALLOC that maps to a non-clearing allocator, calloc would return uninitialized heap memory (info disclosure). This requires a build-time configuration the containing project does not use and cannot be triggered by runtime attacker input.

Dismissed (STEP 4, candidate 4): lib_bounds_set and the library-bound globals are unsynchronized statics; concurrent first calls could run GC_init_lib_bounds twice. This is idempotent, writes identical values, and the failure direction is conservative (uncollectable allocation), so it is a robustness note, not a vulnerability.

Dismissed (STEP 4, candidate 6): if GC_SIZE_MAX equals SIZE_MAX and the underlying allocator internally adds header bytes to the requested size without its own bound check, a near-SIZE_MAX request could overflow downstream. That arithmetic is outside this code and cannot be verified from this listing.

verdict.summary: This GPU FusedBatchNorm Compute implementation validates every attacker-influenced intake at its trust boundary before any sink: x's dimensionality (4 or 5), the reshape path via a return-value-guarded CopyFrom, 1-dimensionality of scale/offset/estimated_mean/estimated_variance, element-count equality (or intentional emptiness) with the channel dimension, and side_input shape equality with the (post-reshape) x that is actually passed to the compute functor. No unvalidated attacker data reaches memory indexing, allocation sizing, or output writes in this code; remaining concerns (dtype enforcement, attribute validation, int64 overflow requiring unallocatable tensors) are either structurally enforced by the framework outside this function or unreachable with states this code permits.

assumptions: OP_REQUIRES aborts the op (error-exit control flow) when its condition fails, so no execution continues past a failed check.

Tensor dtypes match the op registration because the kernel is instantiated for concrete T/U types and the framework only dispatches matching tensors; dtype re-validation inside this function is therefore not required.
Tensor::CopyFrom returns false without modifying the tensor when element counts differ, and supports self-copy (the x.CopyFrom(x,dest_shape) / y->CopyFrom(*y,x_shape) idiom).
A context input tensor cannot have on the order of 2^63 elements, so in_rows * in_cols as int64 cannot overflow for any tensor that reaches this code.
Kernel attributes (tensor_format_, exponential_avg_factor_, is_training_, activation_mode_, has_side_input_) are validated in the kernel constructor, which is not part of this snippet.
limitations: Candidate: side_input shape mismatch could cause OOB access in the downstream functor — rejected; side_input->shape() == x.shape() is enforced before the functor call.
Candidate: scale/offset size mismatch — rejected; NumElements == num_channels enforced for both before the functor call.
Candidate: estimated_mean/estimated_variance size mismatch — rejected; 'empty or num_channels' is enforced, and the empty case is intended op contract handled downstream.
Candidate: x with dims other than 4/5 — rejected; dims check at entry.
Candidate: int64 overflow in in_rows * in_cols during 5-D reshape — rejected as unreachable given tensor allocation limits.
Candidate: channel-multiple-of-4 check omitted on the inference branch — recorded as a documented, path-specific cudnn requirement (see in-code note), not a demonstrated defect.

Candidate: dtype and attribute (exponential_avg_factor_) validation — not present in this snippet; enforced by op registration and the kernel constructor respectively, outside this code's responsibility.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow: sscanf(optarg, "%s", dr) copies an unbounded attacker-controlled command-line option argument into a 10-byte stack buffer char dr[10], with no width specifier or length check. Any -s/-f/-b/-l option argument longer than 9 non-whitespace bytes overwrites the stack frame, enabling control-flow hijacking.

evidence.reason: Root cause: unbounded "%s" conversion in sscanf writes optarg (arbitrary-length CLI option string crossing a trust boundary) into the fixed 10-byte stack buffer dr with no width limit or prior length validation. Trigger: `faad -s AAAAAAAA...(>9 chars) file.aac` reaches case 's' and smashes the stack before atoi() runs. The identical unguarded pattern also exists in case 'f' (line 106), case 'b' (line 120), and case 'l' (line 134); this evidence covers the representative sink at lines 94-95.

assumptions: Command-line arguments are treated as attacker-influenced input per the trust-boundary model (e.g., wrapper scripts, batch frontends, or GUI shells may invoke faad with argument strings derived from untrusted filenames/metadata).
Compile-time macros (LC, MAIN, LTP, LD, FAAD_FMT_16BIT, file_ext) are assumed to define valid constants as in upstream faad2.
limitations: Unchecked fread return (line 265): reading a file shorter than 8 bytes leaves header[8] uninitialized; the garbage bytes only affect mp4-vs-AAC detection and ungetc pushback. Robustness issue, not memory safety in this code.
Eight consecutive ungetc calls (stdin path) exceed the one-character pushback guaranteed by the C standard; on some platforms header bytes are dropped. Portability/robustness issue only.
Memory leaks on early `return 1` error paths after successful malloc; single-shot process with no exhaustion path.
Potential floating-point division by zero when clock() resolution makes dec_length 0; prints inf/NaN, no crash (float math).
Duplicate long-option entry {"stdio",0,0,'g'} shadowed by the earlier {"stdio",0,0,'w'}: `--stdio` cannot set noGapless (use -g). Functional bug, no security impact.
argv[0]/argc==0 pathological environments could make progName NULL or the optind guard vacuous, but that requires the host environment to violate the C main() contract.

verdict.summary: In r_bin_java_rti_annotations_attr_new, the attacker-parsed 16-bit annotation count is stored into the union member attr->info.annotation_array.num_annotations (line 11), but the parse loop's bound on line 14 reads attr->info.rtv_annotations_attr.num_annotations, a different union member that this function never initializes. The loop therefore iterates under control of uninitialized/mismatched union state instead of the parsed value, and the annotations list is likewise stored under a member inconsistent with attr->type, so all type-tagged downstream consumers (size computation, typed teardown/free of the annotations list) access the wrong union member. Trigger: any crafted class file containing a RuntimeInvisibleAnnotations attribute satisfying buf_offset+32 < sz, e.g., an attribute early in a class file with sufficient trailing bytes, causes parsing to proceed with a type-confused/uninitialized loop count on attacker-supplied data.

evidence.reason: The loop bound is read from union member rtv_annotations_attr.num_annotations, which this function never assigns; the parsed attacker-supplied count was written to a different member, attr->info.annotation_array.num_annotations (line 11), and the annotations list to annotation_array.annotations (line 13). The iteration count is therefore uninitialized/type-confused union state (at most accidentally aliased), reachable from any class file whose RuntimeInvisibleAnnotations attribute passes the buf_offset+32 < sz check — a type-confusion/use-of-uninitialized-value defect in this code.

assumptions: buffer points at the start of this attribute with sz bytes remaining, and buf_offset is the absolute file offset (standard radare2 java attr_new calling convention), which makes the line-4 check fail-closed rather than fail-open.

The union members annotation_array and rtv_annotations_attr are distinct types of the RBinJavaAttrInfo info union; if their layouts are byte-identical and the attribute allocation is zeroed, the impact degrades to a parsing inconsistency, but the code as written still reads a member it never wrote.
limitations: r_bin_java_annotation_new could theoretically return a non-NULL annotation with size == 0, making offset never advance and producing an infinite loop with unbounded r_list_append (memory exhaustion); this cannot be confirmed or excluded from this snippet because it depends on the callee's contract, so it is not counted as a vulnerability of this code.

The check 'if (buf_offset + 32 >= sz)' compares an absolute file offset against a remaining-size and is over-restrictive (fails closed for attributes deep in large files), which is a correctness quirk, not a memory-safety issue.
Integer overflow of buf_offset + 32 is unreachable because buf_offset is bounded by the attacker file size, not UINT64_MAX.

verdict.summary: continue_send adds the return value of qemu_chr_fe_write directly to ibe->outpos without checking for a negative (error) return. When the external chardev backend fails (e.g., the external BMC peer disconnects/errors), the call returns -1, making outpos negative (e.g., -1 from an initial outpos of 0). Since outpos < outlen then holds, the retry timer re-arms, and the next invocation passes the pointer 'outbuf + outpos' (outbuf - 1) with the inflated length 'outlen - outpos' (outlen + 1) to qemu_chr_fe_write, reading out of bounds before the buffer and transmitting the bytes to the external channel; repeated errors walk the read arbitrarily far backwards through host memory (info disclosure).

evidence.snippet:
ibe->outpos += qemu_chr_fe_write(ibe->chr, ibe->outbuf + ibe->outpos,
                                    ibe->outlen - ibe->outpos);
evidence.reason: The return value of qemu_chr_fe_write is an untrusted, externally influenced input (state of the external IPMI chardev peer) that is added to the buffer offset outpos with no check for a negative error return. On a -1 return with outpos == 0, outpos becomes -1, the branch at line 9 (outpos < outlen) keeps the retry timer armed, and the next invocation of this same statement indexes outbuf - 1 with the inflated length outlen + 1 — an out-of-bounds read whose contents are written out to the external channel; each additional error decrements outpos further, extending the out-of-bounds read. Root cause: missing validation of the signed return value feeding the buffer index and length (missing bounds enforcement at the memory-read sink).

assumptions: ibe->outpos and ibe->outlen are signed ints, as in the actual QEMU IPMIBmcExtern structure; the negative-offset path requires signed arithmetic.
qemu_chr_fe_write returns ssize_t and can return -1 when the chardev backend errors (peer disconnect, backend failure) — a state reachable by the external BMC peer on the char channel.
The chardev backend (e.g., socket/serial to an external IPMI BMC simulator) is a trust boundary whose observable output includes leaked buffer bytes.
limitations: If outpos were an unsigned type, a -1 return at outpos == 0 would wrap to UINT_MAX, taking the else branch: the failed write would be treated as a fully successful send (waiting_rsp set / sending_cmd cleared as if the external BMC received the message). That fail-open state-advance is a robustness/logic defect with no memory-safety impact in that type configuration.

The repeated 10ms timer retries on persistent write failure constitute an unbounded retry loop and an unbounded backward scan through host memory, but only as an amplifier of the confirmed out-of-bounds read.
Severity is limited to out-of-bounds reads disclosed over the configured chardev; no write primitive past the buffer bounds was identified.

verdict.summary: rpmPackageFilesInstall consumes only pre-validated, index-bounded rpmfi/rpmfs objects; every fdata[fx] access is guarded by rpmfiNext() >= 0 with fdata sized by fc, fp->fpath is assigned for all indices before any later loop can run, file descriptors and iterators are released on all paths, and error handling is fail-closed. No memory-safety, bounds, lifetime, or authz defect is reachable from inputs this code permits.

assumptions: Helper functions (fsmFsPath, fsmMkfile, fsmMkdir, fsmSymlink, fsmMknod, fsmSetmeta, fsmCommit, fsmRemove, ensureDir, rpmpluginsCallFsmFilePre/Post) and the rpmfi/rpmfiles parsing layer perform their documented internal checks; validation of package paths, header indices, and payload entry mapping occurs at the rpmfiles/rpmfi intake layer, which is outside this function.
xcalloc is rpm's overflow-checked allocator and rpmfiFree/Fclose tolerate NULL.
failedFile is non-NULL per the documented rpmpsm caller contract; plugins return 0 on success under normal admin configuration.
limitations: Error-code clobbering: rc = rpmfiStat(...) at the top of the state-collection loop is unconditionally overwritten by rc = rpmpluginsCallFsmFilePre(...); a style/robustness hazard, but rpmfiStat cannot fail with a non-NULL fi, and even a hypothetical failure leaves fp->sb zeroed so the payload dispatch fails closed with RPMERR_UNKNOWN_FILETYPE. Not reachable as a fail-open condition.
No NULL check on failedFile before *failedFile = xstrdup(...); safe under the internal caller contract but would crash a contract-violating caller.

TOCTOU windows between fsmStat/fsmVerify and creation calls exist conceptually, but creation is performed under a transaction-specific suffix and committed via rename, with safe-open logic in the out-of-scope fsm helpers; no exploitable race is provable from this code.
firstlinkfile FD can leak on error exits; resource leak with no exhaustion path in this function.
close(di.dirfd) return value is unchecked; requires a broken environment to matter. Closing fd -1 when the payload loop broke on ensureDir failure is a harmless no-op.

Package-derived modes/rdev passed to fsmMknod/fsmMkfifo/fsmMkdir are trusted per RPM's signed-package threat model; creation-time modes are deliberately restrictive (dirs |= 00700, fifo 0000) with final permissions applied in fsmSetmeta.

verdict.summary: In the empty-match advance path, pos++ is executed unconditionally even when pos == string_lim, so a user-supplied pattern that matches the empty string at the end of the subject (e.g. 'a*') drives pos to string_lim+1. The while (err >= 0) loop never re-checks pos against string_lim, so onig_search is re-invoked with a start pointer beyond the end of the string buffer; for empty-matching patterns the search keeps succeeding at each incremented position, appending the replacement on every iteration, producing an infinite loop with unbounded out_buf growth (memory exhaustion) and, for consuming alternatives, an out-of-bounds read at positions past the subject buffer.

evidence.reason: Missing bounds check on loop-pointer advance (root cause). When oniguruma returns an empty match with pos == string_lim (reachable with attacker-supplied pattern "a*", subject "a", replacement "X": second search at start==range==string_lim returns beg[0]==end[0]==str.size()), the 1-byte append is guarded by 'pos < string_lim' but 'pos++' is not, so pos becomes string_lim+1. The enclosing 'while (err >= 0)' loop condition never validates pos <= string_lim, so onig_search is next called with start = string_lim+1 > end = range = string_lim (violating the sink's requirement that start lie within [str, end]). For empty-matching patterns this repeatedly yields a match at the incremented out-of-range position, appending the replacement each iteration — a non-terminating loop with unbounded out_buf growth; for patterns with consuming alternatives the match attempt at pos > end reads past the subject buffer (out-of-bounds read).

assumptions: php_mb_mbchar_bytes_ex never returns 0 for the configured mbfl encoding, so the replacement walk (p += fwd; i += fwd) always makes progress; if it could return 0, an additional infinite loop would exist in the replacement copy loop.

onig_search performs an empty match at the subject end position when start == range == end (this is the documented/observed behavior of mb_ereg_replace with empty-matching patterns, which is why the pos < string_lim guard on the 1-byte append exists); given that, pos = string_lim+1 is provably produced by this code.

Exact downstream impact (infinite loop / OOM vs. error return) depends on how the oniguruma version handles start > end (start > range selects the backward-search path); the defective state and the out-of-range pointer passed to the search sink are produced by this code as written.
limitations: Backreference append (lines 93-97) was a candidate but is fully guarded: n < regs->num_regs, beg[n] >= 0, beg[n] < end[n], and end[n] <= str.size() are all enforced before the append, so no out-of-bounds access is reachable there.

The non-string pattern path (pat_buf[0] = pattern.toByte(), line 43, marked FIXME 'not multibyte aware') truncates non-string patterns to a single byte; this is a correctness/robustness defect only, with no memory-safety, authz, or fail-open impact.
onig_region_new() return value is not checked for null; failure requires a broken allocation environment (robustness only, no exhaustion path in this code).

verdict.summary: do_rt_sigreturn derives the signal-frame guest pointer by unchecked arithmetic on the fully guest-controlled register env->gpr[1] (line 5). The addition can wrap target_ulong, so a guest invoking rt_sigreturn with r1 near the top of the address space redirects the sigframe access to an arbitrary (wrapped) guest address that still passes the generic guest-range check in lock_user_struct; do_setcontext then parses an attacker-crafted ucontext (registers, signal mask, altstack) from that address, and when the wrapped address is range-valid but unmapped, the host-side read faults in QEMU's own path, crashing the QEMU process. No overflow/range/alignment validation of gpr[1] or of the computed rt_sf_addr is performed in this function.

evidence.reason: env->gpr[1] is attacker-controlled guest register state (guest stack pointer) crossing the guest/QEMU trust boundary. The unchecked unsigned addition can wrap target_ulong (e.g., 64-bit guest with r1 = 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB0 yields rt_sf_addr = 0), and the wrapped value is then used as the base for lock_user_struct/do_setcontext/do_sigaltstack with no range, alignment, or overflow check in this code. Trigger: guest sets r1 near the address-space top and calls rt_sigreturn; a forged sigframe is parsed from the wrapped attacker-chosen address (arbitrary guest-context restoration), and a range-valid-but-unmapped wrapped address causes a fault in QEMU's own code path, aborting the QEMU process. Root cause: integer wraparound (CWE-190) from missing validation of a guest-supplied pointer value.

assumptions: Standard QEMU linux-user semantics: lock_user_struct performs only a generic guest-address-range check on the final (possibly wrapped) value, not on the arithmetic that produced it; for 64-bit guests (and unlimited reserved VA on 64-bit hosts) nearly any wrapped value passes that check.
The guest program is untrusted relative to the QEMU host process, so guest register values are attacker inputs at the guest/host trust boundary.

do_setcontext/do_sigaltstack are separate helpers whose internal validation was assumed present for the altstack address (they perform their own VERIFY_READ lock), but neither re-validates the wrap of the base computed at line 5.
limitations: Candidate C2 (the second derived pointer rt_sf_addr + offsetof(...tuc_stack) passed to do_sigaltstack, lines 10-12) is also wrappable, but the callee performs its own VERIFY_READ lock/validation, so it is not an independent defect in this code.

The ucontext contents (restored registers, signal mask, altstack) being attacker-controlled is inherent sigreturn semantics (the kernel equally parses user memory) and was not counted as a vulnerability; only the unvalidated base address was.

In configurations where guest_base mappings strictly confine all range-valid guest addresses to mapped guest memory, the impact of the wrap is limited to the guest redirecting its own context restoration (guest self-affecting behavior plus potential QEMU process abort on unmapped-but-range-valid addresses); the missing check itself exists in this code as written.
unlock_user_struct on the sigsegv path with rt_sf == NULL is safe because the macro is NULL-checked; not a defect.

verdict.summary: png_zalloc's overflow guard is mathematically sufficient (items <= floor(PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size) implies items*size cannot wrap the 32-bit product), the allocation and PNG_1_0_X memset paths are NULL-checked and length-exact, and all inputs (png_ptr, items, size) originate from libpng/zlib internal state that no attacker-controlled PNG data can influence; the only in-function defects — the read of p->flags before the NULL check and the unchecked size==0 divisor in PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size — are unreachable because libpng always passes its own non-NULL png_struct and zlib only invokes the zalloc callback with positive constant sizes.

assumptions: png_zalloc is installed by libpng as zlib's zalloc callback with libpng's own non-NULL png_struct as the opaque pointer, and zlib invokes it only with fixed positive sizes (struct sizeof values and the fixed 15-bit inflate window), none derived from PNG file contents.

zlib's documented zalloc contract does not require zero-initialized memory; deflate.c and inflate.c explicitly initialize allocated state, and inflate's window accounting (whave) prevents reads of never-written window bytes.
PNG_UINT_32_MAX is 0xffffffff and the multiplication in num_bytes is performed at 32-bit width.
limitations: Unchecked size==0 divisor: 'items > PNG_UINT_32_MAX/size' divides by size with no zero check (CWE-369, crash/DoS). Not reachable: every zlib zalloc call site uses positive constants, and allocation geometry is fixed by libpng at zlib init, not by file data.

Dead NULL guard / deref ordering: 'png_uint_32 save_flags=p->flags;' executes before 'if (png_ptr == NULL)', so a NULL png_ptr would crash at the earlier read and the guard can never fire (CWE-476). Not attacker-reachable: png_ptr is libpng's own opaque value handed to zlib, never NULL.

Non-PNG_1_0_X builds return non-zeroed memory from png_malloc; no uninitialized-memory exposure results because zlib does not require calloc semantics and explicitly initializes the structures it allocates. The PNG_1_0_X path itself is correct (NULL-checked ptr, both memset lengths sum exactly to num_bytes).

If png_malloc fails via longjmp (default mode), p->flags is not restored from save_flags; this is moot because the longjmp abandons the png_struct, and it is not attacker-triggerable beyond OOM conditions.

verdict.summary: flashsv2_prime decompresses attacker-controlled prime data, but every byte it consumes or produces is hard-bounded by zlib's avail_in/avail_out contract, and every length it computes (block_size*3 - avail_out, deflate_block_size - avail_out) is derived from bytes actually written by the previous zlib stage, so no out-of-bounds access is reachable from states this code permits. The attacker-reachable defect is fail-open error handling: the return values of inflate() and deflate() are discarded, so corrupt prime data yields a garbage zlib dictionary and a success return (0), corrupting only the decoded frame with no memory-safety impact. Capacity and length invariants (tmpblock >= 3*block_size, size within src) are enforced at the caller's intake, which this code has no way to re-check.

assumptions: zlib honors its documented API contract: inflate/deflate never read more than avail_in bytes from next_in nor write more than avail_out bytes to next_out, including on error returns such as Z_DATA_ERROR, Z_BUF_ERROR and Z_MEM_ERROR.

The caller (FlashSV bitstream parser) validates size and block_size at intake and allocates s->tmpblock and s->deflate_block with capacities matching (3 * block_size and deflate_block_size respectively), keeping those invariants consistent with the sizes used here.
limitations: Fail-open error handling: the return values of inflate() (lines 14 and 30) and deflate() (line 23) are ignored. An attacker can send a prime block with invalid deflate data; inflate() returns Z_DATA_ERROR, yet the function seeds the decoder's zlib window with garbage and returns 0 (success), so decoding continues with corrupted output. Memory-safe and output corruption only, so not counted as a vulnerability.

No sign or bounds check on the attacker-influenced size parameter before assigning it to avail_in; a negative size would become a huge uInt and cause an out-of-bounds read of the packet buffer. This code cannot produce or detect such a value (no independent length is available here), so the trigger requires the caller's length arithmetic to misbehave; if the caller ever passed a negative size, this would become CWE-125.

No point-of-use capacity check that s->tmpblock actually holds s->block_size * 3 bytes, and s->block_size * 3 is unverified against integer overflow; safe only under the caller's allocation invariant. A caller-side mismatch (tmpblock smaller than 3*block_size) would turn the inflate() writes into a heap buffer overflow (CWE-787), but no such state is reachable from this code as written.
If deflateInit() fails, the function returns -1 without resetting s->zstream, leaving the persistent stream mid-state; robustness-only impact (requires memory exhaustion to trigger).

verdict.summary: The attacker-supplied logout redirect URL (OIDC_REDIRECT_URI_REQUEST_LOGOUT request parameter) is only origin-checked when apr_uri_parse assigns a hostname. If the URL parses successfully with uri.hostname == NULL (e.g. 'https:evil.com/phish' or 'https:/\evil.com', which browsers resolve to the attacker host while APR leaves hostname NULL), the entire same-origin validation is skipped and there is no scheme allowlist; the raw value then flows into the logout redirect sink (directly when no provider end_session_endpoint exists, or embedded as post_logout_redirect_uri otherwise), yielding an open redirect on a network-controlled input.

evidence.reason: The same-origin guard is conjunctively gated on uri.hostname != NULL, so any request-supplied logout URL that apr_uri_parse accepts without a hostname (and no scheme check exists) bypasses origin validation entirely. Trigger: a logged-in victim follows ...?logout=https:evil.com/phish; apr_uri_parse succeeds with hostname NULL, the check is skipped, the CR/LF check passes, and the unvalidated value reaches oidc_handle_logout_request (when the session's provider has no end_session_endpoint) as the redirect Location; the browser resolves 'https:evil.com' to the attacker host, producing an open redirect (CWE-601) rooted in missing input validation (CWE-20).

assumptions: The redirect consumer (browser) parses special-scheme URLs without '//' (e.g. 'https:evil.com/x', 'https:/\evil.com') as pointing to the attacker host per WHATWG URL parsing, while APR's apr_uri_parse leaves uri.hostname NULL for the same strings; this parser differential turns the skipped hostname check into an off-site redirect.

The exploitable direct-redirect path requires provider == NULL or provider->end_session_endpoint == NULL, a configuration state this code explicitly supports; otherwise the unvalidated URL is still embedded (escaped) as post_logout_redirect_uri and forwarded to the provider.
oidc_get_current_url_host returns a non-NULL host string derived from the request, and is treated as the trusted origin reference.
limitations: Potential NULL haystack in strstr(c_host, uri.hostname) if oidc_get_current_url_host could return NULL was dismissed as unreachable given the helper constructs a string from request fields (would otherwise be CWE-476).
The inner shadowed 'const char *error_description' at the apr_uri_parse error branch is a cosmetic shadowing issue with no security effect.
c->default_slo_url is used without validation but originates from administrator configuration (trusted trust boundary).

The front-channel/back-channel dispatch passes 'url' to handlers before any parse-based validation; no defect could be proven without the bodies of oidc_is_front_channel_logout, oidc_is_back_channel_logout and oidc_handle_logout_request, which are outside the given code.

verdict.summary: All attacker-influenced inputs (Mach-O segment/fixup metadata and file bytes) reach only guarded sinks in this function: segment iteration is bounded by both nsegs and segs_count, page_start indexing is preceded by a page_count bound and NULL check, file reads via r_buf_read_at are length-verified, page_size is forced >= 1 before use as a divisor, and all parsed-pointer fields consumed by the callback are assigned on every continuing path. Integer wraps that do occur (page_end_idx, end = start + filesize, cursor arithmetic) cannot produce an out-of-bounds access because each wrap either tightens the loop window or is re-clamped at the next guarded sink.

assumptions: r_buf_read_at performs bounds-checked reads against the underlying buffer and returns the number of bytes actually read, so reads at wrapped/huge cursor values fail the '!= 8' check and terminate the loop.

bin->segs, bin->chained_starts, and chained_starts[i]->page_start are allocated by the Mach-O parsing code consistently with the count fields (segs_count/nsegs, page_count) that this function checks; NULL base pointers are an obj_t construction invariant.
Callers invoke this function only on a fully initialized obj_t and pass limit_start/limit_end ranges (typically section/segment-derived) in the order limit_start <= limit_end.
The RFixup*EventDetails structs are a tagged union with 'type' as the common first member, so the cast to RFixupEventDetails* in the callback dispatch is the intended interface.
limitations: page_end_idx = (R_MIN(limit_end, end) - start) / page_size can underflow to a huge value when segment filesize wraps end below start; harmless here because the page loop breaks at page_count before any page_start access and the inner while requires cursor < end.

cursor <= limit_end - 8 underflows when limit_end < 8, widening the callback dispatch gate; reachable only with a degenerate caller limit range and causes no memory access in this code (offsets still bounded by cursor < limit_end); robustness-only issue for the callback consumer.

delta * stride cursor advance is bounded by the pointer-format bitfield widths (~2^19 * 8), so no ut64 wrap/rewind is reachable; a hypothetically wrapped cursor would still only feed library-clamped reads.

Unvalidated base pointers bin->chained_starts and bin->segs would NULL-deref if a caller invoked this function on an object whose Mach-O lacked the corresponding commands; treated as an internal construction contract, not an input-validation gap in this code.
The unsigned 'default:' pointer-format path silently returns after eprintf, aborting iteration for remaining segments; parsing-completeness behavior only, no security impact.

verdict.summary: XpmCreateDataFromXpmImage never allocates the 'data' buffer: the local 'char **data' is declared uninitialized and no assignment (XpmMalloc/calloc) exists anywhere in the function before its first use at '*data = (char *) (data + data_nlines);'. Control then proceeds to strcpy(*sptr, *sptr2) and CreatePixels/CreateExtensions, which write attacker-influenced header, color, pixel, and extension strings through pointers read from the uninitialized stack variable, and '*data_return = data' publishes the wild pointer. Trigger: any call with a minimally valid, attacker-supplied XPM image (e.g., width=1, height=1, cpp=1, ncolors=1) that passes the existing header_nlines/offset/data_size guards, causing memory corruption (CWE-457, use of uninitialized variable).

evidence.reason: First use of the local variable 'data', which is declared at line 9 and never assigned anywhere in the function (the allocation 'data = XpmMalloc(data_size)' is absent). This statement performs pointer arithmetic on uninitialized stack contents and stores through the uninitialized pointer — a wild write reachable with a minimal valid image (ncolors=1, width=height=cpp=1) that passes all preceding guards.

evidence.snippet:
for (l = 0, sptr = data, sptr2 = header; l <= n && sptr && sptr2; l++, sptr++, sptr2++) {
	strcpy(*sptr, *sptr2);
evidence.reason: The loop guard only checks the slot addresses (sptr, sptr2), not the slot contents. *sptr is read from the never-allocated 'data' array (uninitialized stack memory), and strcpy copies attacker-influenced header/color strings produced by CreateColors into that garbage-derived destination — memory corruption on the same trigger path as the line-102 defect.

assumptions: The XpmImage/XpmInfo contents (width, height, ncolors, cpp, colorTable, extensions) originate from parsing attacker-supplied XPM data (typical libXpm flow: XpmReadFileToXpmImage -> XpmCreateDataFromXpmImage), so they cross a trust boundary that this function must validate itself.
RETURN() behaves as in upstream libXpm (set ErrorStatus and goto exit), and either VOID_SPRINTF variant compiles; the sprintf hints line fits in buf[BUFSIZ] either way.

Lines 91 and 93 are condition-less 'RETURN(XpmNoMemory);' statements — residue of guard conditions (e.g., 'image->height > 0 && offset > UINT_MAX / image->height') whose condition text is missing from this listing. If compiled literally they abort the function early on every input (fail-closed functional break, not a memory-safety guard); the confirmed vulnerability is the missing allocation of 'data', which is present in the code as written regardless.
limitations: XpmCalloc(header_size, sizeof(char *)) at line 38 over-allocates by 4x because header_size already includes sizeof(char *) — wasteful but not a safety defect.
The duplicated 'if(offset <= ... )' (lines 83-84) and duplicated 'data_size += image->height * offset;' (lines 92/94) are redundant, not independently exploitable.

The 'l <= n' loop writes *(sptr + 1) = data[ncolors + 1], which in the upstream design is the legitimate data[header_nlines] slot reserved for the first pixel-line pointer — not an out-of-bounds write in the intended buffer layout (moot here since the buffer is never allocated).
XpmFree(header) at line 134 is indented as if inside the for loop but executes once after it, inside 'if (header)' — behavior is correct; style issue only.
Unchecked effects of the early fail-closed stray RETURNs (if taken literally) would constitute a functional denial of service of this API, not a memory-safety vulnerability.

verdict.summary: smtp_mailaddr() processes attacker-controlled SMTP address strings but validates them at intake: it checks NULL and '<'/'>' framing, branches on the parser's failure return, and applies valid_localpart/valid_domainpart to every accepted non-empty user and domain before use (fail-closed). The only non-obvious memory sink, memmove(maddr->user, p, strlen(p) + 1) where p points just past a ':' inside maddr->user, is provably in-bounds for every reachable input: p is strchr's result plus one, so it never passes the field's NUL terminator, and strlen(p)+1 never exceeds the field's remaining capacity, which equals the destination capacity since the destination starts at the field's first byte; overlap is handled by memmove. strlcpy uses sizeof of the array member, and the early return(1) for the empty sender is the RFC 5321-required null return path, not a fail-open bypass. No reachable trigger produces an out-of-bounds access, injection, or authorization bypass in this code as written.

assumptions: text_to_mailaddr() fills the fixed-size struct mailaddr fields with bounds-checked, NUL-terminated copies (strlcpy/length checks in the same codebase) and returns 0 on overflow or failure; its return value is checked here, and maddr is zeroed by that callee before this function reads maddr->user/maddr->domain.
valid_localpart() and valid_domainpart() validate character sets and syntax of the attacker-derived user and domain strings; this code applies both before accepting any non-empty address.

Callers (SMTP command handlers) always pass a writable buffer as `line` (the session's command buffer) and a non-NULL out-pointer as `args`, per the documented signature; this code's only writes through those are within the string and through the valid out-pointer.

`domain` is the local server's configured domain (trusted configuration), not runtime attacker data; a misconfigured overlong domain would cause silent truncation and then rejection by valid_domainpart, with no memory-safety impact.
limitations: Candidate dismissed: memmove(maddr->user, p, strlen(p)+1) after strchr(':') — attacker-chosen localpart containing ':' is reachable, but the source pointer cannot pass the field's NUL terminator and the length cannot exceed the destination capacity, so no out-of-bounds state is reachable (e.g., trigger 'MAIL FROM:<route:user@domain>' copies only the in-bounds suffix).

Candidate dismissed: the discarded strlcpy return for the default domain is a robustness/correctness issue only (silent truncation of a trusted, misconfigured domain), not attacker-reachable memory unsafety.
Candidate dismissed: early return(1) for an empty sender (MAIL FROM:<>) is required RFC 5321 bounce behavior; it bypasses no validation for non-empty addresses and grants no privilege.
Candidate dismissed: ':'-stripping silently rewrites 'a:b@c' to 'b@c'; this is a prefix strip of the attacker's own address that then undergoes normal validation, with no authorization bypass.
Candidate dismissed: NULL `args` or read-only `line` triggers require callers to violate the documented contract; no path in this code permits those states.

Behavior of text_to_mailaddr/valid_localpart/valid_domainpart was treated per their contracts in this codebase since their bodies are not included; if any of them failed to bound or NUL-terminate its output, the defect would reside in that callee, not in this function.

verdict.summary: Stack buffer overflow in the FORMAT_DOUBLE handling of dprintf_formatf: the precision-clamping heuristic uses an unsigned size_t counter (maxprec) that decrements once per integer-part digit of the double; for values >= 10^(BUFFSIZE-2) (e.g., 1e300) the counter underflows and wraps to a huge value, so the clamp never fires. (sprintf)(work, formatbuf, p->data.dnum) then renders a number with an integer part far larger than work[BUFFSIZE], writing hundreds of bytes past the end of the stack buffer. Trigger: curl_mprintf-style call such as format "%.5f" with attacker-influenced double value 1e300.

evidence.reason: Unbounded sprintf into the fixed-size stack buffer work[BUFFSIZE] using a format spec (formatbuf) whose precision was supposed to be clamped to fit work. With a double like 1e300 and any precision (e.g. "%.5f"), the rendered integer part alone (~301 digits) exceeds the buffer, causing an out-of-bounds stack write (CWE-787). No length check guards this sink; the CURLDEBUG assert below only fires in debug builds and only after the overflow already occurred.

The only precision clamp uses an unsigned size_t counter decremented once per integer-part digit of the attacker-influenced double. For |dnum| >= 10^(BUFFSIZE-2) (e.g., 1e300 gives 301 iterations against 126), maxprec underflows and wraps to a huge value, so the subsequent 'if(prec > maxprec)' clamp at the next lines never triggers, allowing sprintf to overflow work. This is the integer-underflow root cause (CWE-191) enabling the out-of-bounds write at the sprintf sink.

assumptions: BUFFSIZE is the standard curl value 128 (the underflow trigger only requires a double with more than BUFFSIZE-2 integer digits, and DBL_MAX has 309, so the finding holds for any realistic BUFFSIZE).
dprintf_Pass1 validates format-string structure and vto[] indices (it returns -1 on failure), so parameter indexing is assumed sound.
The format string literal itself is caller/trusted (as with any printf-style API); the attacker-influenced inputs are the variadic data arguments, notably the double in FORMAT_DOUBLE.
limitations: FORMAT_INTPTR ('%n'-style) writes 'done' to a caller-supplied pointer; this is the documented printf %n feature and only becomes an arbitrary write if the caller lets an attacker control the format string itself — not a defect of this code under its intended contract.
FORMAT_STRING relies on caller-supplied strings being NUL-terminated when no precision is given (strlen); violating that C-string contract is a caller-side bug.

A secondary candidate exists in FORMAT_INT: a precision supplied via a variadic parameter ('%.*d', FLAGS_PRECPARAM) is not clamped to the buffer size, so 'while(prec-- > 0) *w-- = '0'' could write backwards past work[0] with a huge positive precision parameter; it was not promoted to primary evidence because the code path depends on dprintf_Pass1's handling of PRECPARAM for integer conversions, which is external to this snippet.
In non-CURLDEBUG builds the assert after sprintf is compiled out, so the release build has no detection of the overflow at all.

verdict.summary: No reachable security vulnerability found. All indexed reads of the command string stay within the NUL-terminated buffer; the case ' '/'+' concatenation allocates strlen(comment)+strlen(newcomment)+2 bytes and only ever appends the unescaped copy nc, which r_str_unescape guarantees is never longer than newcomment, so the buffer is always sufficient; all format strings are compile-time constants with attacker data only in %s arguments; sdb_decode output is heap-allocated with a zeroed terminator; r_num_math results are used only as metadata addresses, never as memory indices or sizes.

assumptions: r_str_unescape operates in place and maps every escape sequence (\n, \xNN, etc.) from N source bytes to at most N output bytes, so strlen(nc) <= strlen(newcomment) always holds.

The caller (cmd_meta) dispatches this function only for commands beginning with 'C', so input points to a NUL-terminated string of at least one character; reads of input[1..3] therefore never pass the terminator.
sdb_decode allocates strlen(input)+1 zeroed bytes and base64 output is strictly shorter than its input, so the returned buffer is NUL-terminated.
limitations: Case ' '/'+' builds an undo redo-command via r_str_newf("CC %s@0x%08"PFMT64x, nc, addr) without escaping the comment text; a comment containing r2 command syntax (';', '@', newlines) would be re-interpreted as commands when undo is replayed. This is in-process command injection into the same interpreter the command text already controls (no privilege boundary crossing in radare2's threat model), so it is not counted as a vulnerability.

In case 'CCf-', 'int i' is compared against the wider bb->size; a basic block larger than INT_MAX would cause signed overflow of i and metadata deletion at wrapped addresses, but such a block is not producible by this code and the effect is not memory-unsafe.
strdup(newcomment) in case ' '/'+' and strdup(s+1) in case 'a' are not checked for NULL before use; only reachable under allocator failure (robustness, not security).
getcommapath/core allocation failures could pass NULL to r_cons_printf %s; OOM-only, robustness.
If a future version of r_str_unescape could expand strings, the malloc/strcat sequence in case ' '/'+' would become a heap overflow; with the current shrink-only semantics it is in-bounds.

verdict.summary: flashsv2_prime() ignores the return values of both inflate() calls on attacker-controlled compressed priming data (src/size). When the attacker supplies a corrupted or truncated zlib stream, inflate() fails (e.g., Z_DATA_ERROR) yet the function continues through the deflate round-trip and returns 0 (success). The caller then trusts that s->zstream was primed and s->tmpblock holds valid data, causing downstream decoding to operate on an unprimed dictionary and uninitialized/partially-initialized tmpblock contents — a fail-open input-validation gap leading to use of uninitialized memory.

evidence.reason: The return value of the first inflate() on attacker-supplied priming data (src, size) is discarded. Trigger: a FlashSV2 block whose priming bytes form an invalid zlib stream makes inflate() return Z_DATA_ERROR, yet execution continues to line 30 and returns 0, so the caller trusts a dictionary priming that never happened and subsequently uses uninitialized/inconsistent s->tmpblock and zstream state (use of uninitialized memory / fail-open on trust-boundary data).

The second inflate(), fed data derived from the attacker-influenced round-trip (which can be truncated if deflate_block_size is insufficient), is also unchecked; the function unconditionally reports success even when this re-inflation fails, leaving s->zstream in a state the caller cannot distinguish from a successful prime.

assumptions: s->block_size, s->tmpblock (block_size*3 bytes), s->deflate_block and s->deflate_block_size are allocated consistently by the decoder outside this snippet, so the in-function avail_out arithmetic cannot exceed buffer bounds; this assumption could not be verified from the given code alone.

The caller of flashsv2_prime treats a return value of 0 as confirmation that the zlib dictionary was primed and subsequently decodes using s->zstream/s->tmpblock, which is how the unchecked inflate failures translate into use of uninitialized memory.
limitations: deflate() (line 19) and deflateEnd() (line 20) return values are unchecked; however, avail_out arithmetic still matches exactly the bytes written, so this is a robustness issue without a memory-safety trigger in this code.

A negative 'size' or overflowing s->block_size*3 would corrupt the uInt avail_in/avail_out computations, but both require the packet parser/allocation path outside this function to violate its contract; not reachable from this code as written.
The early return -1 after a failed deflateInit leaves s->zstream mid-inflate; caller is expected to treat any non-zero return as failure — contract issue only.

verdict.summary: GlyphCache::Loader reads the attacker-controlled numGlyphs count from the maxp table of a font and passes `_num_glyphs_graphics-1` to TtfUtil::LocaLookup without checking that the count is nonzero. A font whose maxp declares numGlyphs == 0 (with a glyf table present, so the `_glyf` short-circuit does not skip the call) makes the expression wrap to an invalid glyph id (0xFFFFFFFF as an unsigned index). The only guard is a post-hoc comparison against a single sentinel, `== size_t(-2)`, so the underflowed id reaches the loca-table lookup and any non-(-2) result is accepted, enabling an out-of-bounds loca access (crash/DoS) when a malicious font is loaded.

evidence.reason: `_num_glyphs_graphics` is assigned directly from TtfUtil::GlyphCount(maxp) on line 19 with no check that it is nonzero; the subtraction `_num_glyphs_graphics-1` therefore underflows to -1 (0xFFFFFFFF as the unsigned glyph id) when the attacker-controlled maxp numGlyphs field is 0 and a glyf table exists. The sink TtfUtil::LocaLookup requires a valid glyph index, but this code never enforces `_num_glyphs_graphics >= 1` before the call — it only inspects the return value afterwards and rejects exactly one sentinel (size_t(-2)), accepting every other outcome with the wrapped index. Trigger: malicious font with numGlyphs == 0 and a glyf table reaches line 21 directly (lines 13/17 pass), producing the invalid id at the lookup sink.

assumptions: TtfUtil::LocaLookup indexes the loca table using the supplied glyph id; if its internal bounds check computes `glyph_id + 1` or `glyph_id * 2 + 2` in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, the wrapped id 0xFFFFFFFF bypasses it and causes an out-of-bounds read. If it validates in 64-bit arithmetic it would return size_t(-2) and the load would fail cleanly, reducing impact to a robustness issue; the missing zero-check in this code is the root defect either way.
`_num_glyphs_graphics` is an unsigned integer type of at least 16 bits holding the maxp numGlyphs value (0..65535).
limitations: m_pGloc underflow in the tmpnumgattrs computation (lines 42-45): size_t wraparound is possible, but every reachable wrapped value truncates to a negative int (low 32 bits >= 0xFFFF0000 for _num_attrs <= 65535) and is rejected by `tmpnumgattrs < 0` on line 47; dismissed as guarded.

No minimum-size check on the maxp table before TtfUtil::GlyphCount(maxp) (line 17/19) — `if (!maxp)` checks presence only, unlike the explicit size checks for Gloc (>= 8) and Glat (>= 4). Whether a truncated maxp causes an OOB read depends on GlyphCount's implementation (it receives no size argument), so this cannot be confirmed from the given code.

`int version` receiving a uint32 (lines 35, 58): a Glat/Gloc version with the high bit set becomes negative and passes the `>= 0x00040000` / `>= 0x00020000` rejection tests; no security-relevant sink is reachable within this constructor on that path (robustness only).
The hard-coded `_has_boxes = true` workaround (lines 68-69) is a functional workaround, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: The function is the fully-mitigated form of FFmpeg's ff_h264_pred_weight_table. Every value this code takes from the bitstream is validated before its sink: luma/chroma log2 weight denominators are checked against 7U (an unsigned compare that also traps negative get_ue_golomb error values) before the '1 << denom' shifts, and all parsed weights are round-tripped through int8_t and rejected via out_range_weight/AVERROR_INVALIDDATA before being stored. The only unguarded dimension is ref_count[list], which bounds array indices i and 16+2*i; no out-of-bounds state can be produced from this code alone because the array dimensions are external and the producer of ref_count (the slice-header parser in the same decoder trust domain) constrains num_ref_idx per the documented contract. Residual issues (stale/uninitialized chroma_log2_weight_denom read and uninitialized chroma_weight copy when chroma_format_idc==0, and fail-open clamping of bad denominators) are sanitized before any sink or confined to never-consumed fields, with no security impact.

assumptions: H264PredWeightTable's luma_weight/chroma_weight arrays (declared externally in h264_parse.h) are dimensioned to accommodate the maximum reference counts the caller can pass, including the 16+2*i field-expansion indices for PICT_FRAME.

ref_count[list] is produced by the H.264 slice-header parser in the same decoder trust domain, which constrains num_ref_idx to the H.264 maximum before this function is called; this function's contract is that ref_count is pre-validated.
get_ue_golomb/get_se_golomb/get_bits1 behave per the FFmpeg golomb-reader contract; negative get_ue_golomb error returns are handled correctly by the unsigned '> 7U' comparisons.
pwt points to a caller-owned struct that may retain stale values from previously decoded slices.
limitations: Dismissed candidate (OOB write): the loop bound ref_count[list] and the 16+2*i / 16+2*i+1 indices (lines 26 and 65-72) are not bounds-checked inside this function. A trigger cannot be constructed from the given code because the array dimensions are not part of it; reaching an out-of-bounds index requires the caller to pass a reference count exceeding the array capacity, violating the documented producer contract. In the real codebase the slice-header parser constrains num_ref_idx and the weight arrays are sized for the permitted maximum.

Dismissed candidate (uninitialized/stale read): when chroma_format_idc == 0, pwt->chroma_log2_weight_denom is never assigned but is read by the '> 7U' check (line 17), and the PICT_FRAME block (lines 69-70) copies never-written chroma_weight[i] entries into the 16+2*i slots. The read value is sanitized into [0,7] and the derived chroma_def is unused in that configuration; the copied garbage is never consumed because use_weight_chroma/chroma_weight_flag remain 0 for monochrome streams. Robness/MSan noise only, no security impact.

Dismissed candidate (fail-open handling): out-of-range luma/chroma denominators are logged and clamped to 0 rather than aborting the slice (lines 13-20). The substituted value is fully constrained to [0,7] before the only sink (the shift), so no attacker-controlled value reaches a sensitive sink; this is spec-tolerance behavior, not a fail-open of a security decision.

Dismissed candidate (shift/weight range): '1 << luma_log2_weight_denom' and the weight stores are guarded by the unsigned >7U checks and the int8_t round-trip checks respectively; verified by reading both branches, including the negative-return case from get_ue_golomb which the unsigned comparison traps.
