verdict.summary: dprintf_formatf writes attacker-influenced width/precision values into memory without any bounds checks. In FORMAT_DOUBLE, curl_msnprintf's return value (the untruncated length) advances fptr past the end of the 32-byte formatbuf, after which the flag/conversion/NUL byte stores write out of bounds; additionally the 'left' size was computed before up to four flag bytes were consumed and is never clamped. Independently, the constructed formatbuf (which can legally contain a 19-digit width or a large precision such as '%9223372036854775807f' or '%.99999999f') is passed to an unbounded sprintf targeting the fixed-size stack buffer work[BUFFSIZE], producing a massive stack overflow. In FORMAT_INT, the precision zero-fill loop writes backward from workend without bounding prec, smashing the stack below work[0]. All triggers are reachable with constant format strings and attacker-influenced data arguments (e.g., '%*f' or '%.*d' with a huge * value), so the bugs do not depend on an attacker-controlled format string.

evidence.snippet:
len = curl_msnprintf(fptr, left, ".%ld", prec);
           fptr += len;
evidence.reason: curl_msnprintf returns the number of characters that would have been written, not the truncated count, and 'left' was computed at line 332 before up to four flag bytes were consumed at lines 348-354, so it overstates the remaining space in the 32-byte formatbuf. Advancing fptr by this unclamped length can place fptr past formatbuf[31]; the subsequent unconditional stores '*fptr++ = l' (line 370), the conversion character (lines 373/375/377) and '*fptr = 0' (line 379) then write out of bounds. Trigger: constant format "%-+ #*.*lf" with data arguments width=99999999 and precision=9223372036854775807 puts fptr at formatbuf[33] before the OOB stores. Root cause: missing bound/clamp on fptr (and left) before the memory writes; attacker-influenced width/precision data crossing the va_list trust boundary reach this sink unvalidated.

Unbounded sprintf into the fixed-size stack buffer char work[BUFFSIZE]. formatbuf can legally hold an attacker-influenced field width of up to 19 digits or a large precision (e.g., "%9223372036854775807f" or "%.99999999f" built from a '%*f'/'%.*f' data argument), and nothing on this path bounds the resulting output to sizeof(work). sprintf then emits up to ~9.2e18 padding bytes (or ~1e8 precision digits) into work, a deterministic stack buffer overflow. Root cause: missing check that the formatted output fits work[BUFFSIZE] before the copy; the unvalidated width/precision crossing the va_list trust boundary drive the length.

The precision zero-fill loop writes backward from workend = &work[BUFFSIZE-2] with prec taken raw from attacker-influenced data (line 119 via FLAGS_PRECPARAM '%.*d', or the parsed literal precision at line 128). No check enforces prec <= workend - work, so a large precision writes far below work[0], corrupting the stack. Trigger: constant format "%.*d" with precision argument 9999999 and any integer value produces ~10^7 out-of-bounds backward stores. Root cause: missing bounds check on prec at the memory-write sink.

assumptions: dprintf_Pass1 (not shown) is assumed to pass width/precision values (both literal digits and '*' argument values) through without capping them; this code re-reads the raw values at lines 103/119/339/345 and performs no bounds enforcement of its own at the sinks. If Pass1 caps width/precision to a small value, findings at lines 207-208 and 383 would be mitigated, and the formatbuf overflow at 366-367 would require literal format contents; as written, no such cap is visible.
BUFFSIZE is a compile-time constant smaller than achievable formatted output (e.g., 256); work is a plain stack array with no overflow detection.

curl_msnprintf is assumed to follow the printf-family convention of returning the length that would have been written without truncation (this is its documented curl behavior), which is what makes 'fptr += len' exceed the buffer.
Line numbers were counted from the first line of the presented function body (line 1 = 'static int dprintf_formatf(').
limitations: FORMAT_INTPTR (lines 393-401) writes through p->data.ptr taken from the va_list; this is the documented %n-style semantics of this printf-family API, and abusing it requires the caller to pass an attacker-controlled format string, violating the printf contract. Not counted as a vulnerability in this code, though callers must never forward untrusted formats.

The width-padding loops (OUTCHAR) can emit huge output through the caller-supplied stream function; for the msnprintf wrapper the stream truncates at the destination size, so this is a robustness/DoS-at-worst concern in the caller's stream, not a memory-safety defect in this code.

vto[param] indexing at line 99 could go out of bounds only if dprintf_Pass1 accepts a positional specifier beyond MAX_PARAMETERS; the code checks Pass1's error return at line 35, so this is dismissed as Pass1's validated contract (unverifiable from the given code).
width/prec padding relies on OUTCHAR; an unchecked stream failure would only degrade output, not memory safety.
The negative-minimum handling in FORMAT_INT (lines 172-175) is a correct workaround for INTMIN negation; no integer-overflow defect found there.

verdict.summary: The NFSv3 WRITE argument decoder validates the attacker-controlled header against the head iovec, requires count==len, verifies the received data length (dlen) is at least the declared length, and clamps count/len to svc_max_payload before building the write vectors; the vector loop is therefore bounded by RPCSVC_MAXPAGES capacity and no reachable memory-safety, bounds, or validation flaw exists in this code as written.

assumptions: The RPC receive layer (svc) backs rq_arg.head with page-aligned buffers of at least PAGE_SIZE and caps messages at RPCSVC_MAXPAYLOAD, so max_blocksize ≤ RPCSVC_MAXPAYLOAD and rq_vec/rq_pages (RPCSVC_MAXPAGES) always have capacity for the clamped len.
RPCSEC/GSS unwrapping may pad the data buffer, which the dlen check intentionally tolerates (dlen may be larger than needed).
limitations: Reads of count/stable/len (and up to ~64 bytes consumed by decode_fh plus 8 by xdr_decode_hyper) occur before the head bound check 'if ((void *)p > head->iov_base + head->iov_len)'; a short message can cause reads a few dozen bytes past head->iov_len. These stay within the page-backed receive buffer, the values are discarded when the check rejects the request, and nothing is echoed back, so this is at most a robustness issue, not a vulnerability.

XDR_QUADLEN(len)*4 wraps for len ≥ 0xFFFFFFFD, making the dlen minimum check trivially pass; however the subsequent count==len invariant plus the max_blocksize clamp forces len down to max_blocksize before any sink, so the wrapped value is never used.

dlen includes tail->iov_len while the write vectors only cover head+pages, so in padded (e.g., GSS) setups the vectors may reference partially-filled pages; this is documented upstream behavior with no memory-safety impact.
args->stable is not range-checked against {0,1,2}; downstream treats any non-zero value as a sync flag — a logic/robustness nit, not a security defect.

verdict.summary: hopen_mem decodes an attacker-controlled data: URL payload (hts_decode_percent / hts_decode_base64) but discards the decode functions' return values and never initializes `length`. On a malformed payload (e.g., an invalid or truncated percent escape such as "%G1" or a trailing "%"), decoding fails without this function ever validating the payload or the result, and the potentially uninitialized `length` is passed to hfile_init_fixed as the readable extent of the heap buffer (line 26). The resulting hFILE can then serve out-of-bounds reads of the allocation. This is a fail-open intake-validation gap on data crossing a trust boundary.

evidence.reason: The return value of hts_decode_percent is ignored, and `length` (declared uninitialized at line 3) is set only by this callee. For an attacker-supplied URL like "data:,%G1" with mode "r", the decoder hits an invalid percent escape and fails without this function ever constraining or checking `length`; the unchecked garbage/partial value is then consumed at line 26 (hfile_init_fixed(..., buffer, length, size)) as the readable length of the size-byte heap buffer, enabling out-of-bounds reads. The base64 branch (line 16, hts_decode_base64(buffer, &length, data)) has the identical unchecked pattern. Root cause: fail-open error handling / use of uninitialized value (CWE-457, CWE-252) on a trust-boundary input.

assumptions: `url` crosses a trust boundary: data: URIs in this handler are attacker-influenced (e.g., URIs appearing in attacker-supplied file metadata that the application passes to the file opener).

The decode helpers follow the conventional size_t-returning decode contract: they return 0 / signal failure (errno) for malformed input, and this code's only source for `length` is the callee's `*length` out-param, which this code never checks.

Canonical hts_base64_decoded_length (bound (N/4)*3 + (rem ? rem-1 : 0)) and hts_decode_base64 (emits at most floor(3N/4) bytes, skipping non-alphabet characters) agree, so the base64 allocation bound itself is not exceeded under that implementation.
limitations: C2 (potential base64 size/write mismatch) could not be confirmed: the writer receives no size parameter, but under the canonical helper pair the allocation bound is exact-or-generous for every input length, so no concrete overflowing trigger was constructible from this code alone.
C3: `size` can be 0 (empty payload) making `malloc(0)` implementation-defined; decoders then write 0 bytes — robustness only, no security impact.
C4: integer overflow of `strlen(data)+1` or `hts_base64_decoded_length` would require an input near SIZE_MAX bytes, unreachable in practice.
C5: `mode` is caller-supplied and only searched for 'r'; write modes are rejected/unsupported per the TODO comment — no memory-safety path in this function.

Exact severity of the `length` misuse depends on the unseen decoders' error paths; the confirmed defect in this code is the discarded decode status and the unconditional use of the unvalidated `length` at line 26.

verdict.summary: compand_drain reads from the delay buffer through an index wrapped by MOD(dindex+1, s->delay_samples) and writes into a frame allocated with exactly FFMIN(2048, s->delay_count) samples, so both the read cursor and write loop bound stay within their allocations; the allocation result is NULL-checked before use, and the delay_count subtraction cannot underflow because nb_samples is the min of 2048 and delay_count. The dangerous-looking preconditions (delay_samples == 0 with delay_count > 0 causing MOD division by zero, or a NULL/unallocated delay_frame) are self-contradictory states this filter's own configuration and state machine cannot produce: delay_count only becomes positive when samples enter a configured delay line, and with no delay configured nb_samples is 0 so the buffer dereference is never executed. No attacker-influenced input crosses an unvalidated trust boundary into a memory, command, path, or markup sink in this function.

assumptions: s->delay_frame is allocated during filter configuration with at least s->delay_samples double samples per channel plane, using the same channel layout as outlink (this filter does not change channel count between input and output).

s->delay_count is only incremented for samples actually placed into the delay line, which the filter's configuration gates on s->delay_samples > 0; hence the state {delay_count > 0, delay_samples == 0} cannot occur.
compand_drain is invoked by the filter's activate/flush logic in states the filter itself established (i.e., with delay_frame allocated whenever delayed samples exist).
outlink->channels is > 0, as enforced by audio-format negotiation in the filter framework.
limitations: If delay_count were ever allowed to exceed delay_samples (not producible by the shown logic), the MOD wrap would cause emission of stale/already-output samples — an in-bounds correctness defect, not a memory-safety issue.

If compand_drain were called with delay_count == 0 in a loop keyed on successful drain returns, empty frames would be produced repeatedly; the shown code itself terminates correctly (nb_samples 0, delay_count unchanged), and the termination condition belongs to the caller.
The declaration 'int chan, i, dindex;' leaves dindex uninitialized; it would be stored to s->delay_index uninitialized only if channels == 0, which the framework prevents.

A negative delay_count would produce a failed allocation (rejected by the sample-buffer sizing helper), which is handled by the existing NULL check and ENOMEM return — robust behavior, not a vulnerability.

verdict.summary: write_refcount_block_entries() rounds last_index up to a sector boundary ((last_index + REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR) & ~(REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR - 1)) and computes the write length from it, then passes &s->refcount_block_cache[first_index] and that length to bdrv_pwrite without ever checking that the rounded extent stays within the refcount block (first_index/last_index <= REFCOUNTS_PER_BLOCK, the capacity of the cluster-sized refcount_block_cache buffer). With attacker-influenced qcow2 geometry or a bound at the block edge, the round-up exceeds the cache capacity, so bdrv_pwrite reads out of bounds of the heap buffer and writes past the end of the refcount block in the image, leaking heap contents into the attacker-supplied image and corrupting adjacent metadata.

evidence.reason: The sink reads `size` bytes starting at &s->refcount_block_cache[first_index] where size = (last_index - first_index) << REFCOUNT_SHIFT was computed from last_index after it was rounded UP past the caller-supplied value ((last_index + REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR) & ~(REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR - 1)). No check in this code clamps the rounded last_index (or first_index) to REFCOUNTS_PER_BLOCK, the capacity of the cluster-sized refcount_block_cache buffer. Trigger: an untrusted qcow2 image / guest-driven refcount update producing last_index at the refcount block boundary (or geometry with REFCOUNTS_PER_BLOCK < REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR); the round-up then exceeds the block, and bdrv_pwrite performs an out-of-bounds read of the cache buffer (contents written into the attacker-readable image file) plus a write beyond the refcount block's end.

assumptions: The qcow2 image file (header geometry, refcount table) is treated as untrusted input crossing a trust boundary, as is normal for QEMU block drivers; first_index/last_index ultimately derive from guest I/O offsets and image geometry.
REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR is 512 >> REFCOUNT_SHIFT and refcount_block_cache holds exactly one refcount block (cluster_size bytes), so the required bound at the sink is last_index <= REFCOUNTS_PER_BLOCK.
The code was received truncated after `return ret;`; analysis covers exactly the lines shown.
limitations: Candidate dismissed: integer overflow in `last_index + REFCOUNTS_PER_SECTOR` requires indices near INT_MAX, which masked cluster-index arithmetic cannot produce — unreachable.

Candidate noted: the `if (cache_refcount_updates)` gating places the sector-aligned write on the caching path only; with the snippet truncated, the non-caching path cannot be inspected, so any fail-open/persistence issue there is unconfirmed (robustness/correctness concern).

Candidate noted: refcount_block_offset (parsed from the image refcount table) is used directly as the write offset with no alignment/bounds validation in this function; if the table-loading path does not validate entries, an arbitrary-offset write into the image is possible — the responsible intake validation is outside the shown code.

If callers provably pass only inclusive in-range indices AND cluster_bits >= 9 is enforced elsewhere, the overshoot is not reachable; this code itself enforces neither precondition, which is the basis of the finding.

verdict.summary: GlyphCache::Loader trusts the attacker-controlled maxp numGlyphs value without checking it for zero, then computes _num_glyphs_graphics-1 (line 21): when numGlyphs is 0 this underflows size_t to SIZE_MAX, which is passed as a glyph index to TtfUtil::LocaLookup, defeating the intended 'wildly out of range' sanity check (an (index+1)-based range check wraps) and allowing an invalid index to reach table indexing. Additionally, table version fields read as uint32 are stored into a signed int (lines 37, 60); version values with the high bit set (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFF) compare negative, bypassing the 'reject Glat tables that are too new' and Gloc version gates — a fail-open validation bypass on font data.

evidence.reason: _num_glyphs_graphics is the raw numGlyphs value read from the attacker-controlled maxp table at line 19 with no zero/range check at this intake boundary. When numGlyphs == 0 (a state this code permits), _num_glyphs_graphics-1 promotes to int -1 and converts to size_t SIZE_MAX. That value is passed as the glyph index to TtfUtil::LocaLookup, whose glyph-range sanity check this line relies on; SIZE_MAX is an invalid glyph index that an (index+1)-based bounds check cannot reject, so the gate fails open and the huge index reaches loca-table indexing (out-of-bounds table access). Root cause: CWE-191 integer underflow from the missing validation of the attacker-supplied glyph count before subtraction.

evidence.snippet:
version = be::read<uint32>(p);
        if (version >= 0x00040000 || (version >= 0x00030000 && m_pGlat.size() < 8))       // reject Glat tables that are too new
evidence.reason: The Glat version is read as uint32 but stored in the signed 'int version'; any attacker-chosen version with the high bit set (e.g. 0xFFFFFFFF) becomes a negative int, so both 'too new' thresholds evaluate false and a table declaring an unknown/future version is accepted and later parsed as a legacy (v1/v2, _has_boxes=false) table, defeating the explicit rejection gate. The same defect affects the Gloc version read into 'int version' at line 37 and checked at line 49. Root cause: CWE-196 unsigned-to-signed conversion enabling fail-open version validation on font data.

assumptions: TtfUtil::GlyphCount returns the raw uint16 numGlyphs field from the attacker-supplied maxp table (0..65535) with no additional lower-bound validation at this intake point.

TtfUtil::LocaLookup validates the glyph index with an (index+1)-times-entry-size comparison against the loca table length, which wraps to 0 for SIZE_MAX; under that standard implementation the underflowed index reaches out-of-bounds table indexing. If LocaLookup instead rejects SIZE_MAX with the -2 sentinel, the font is merely rejected and impact is limited to the validation logic itself.
limitations: The tmpnumgattrs computation (lines 44-47) can underflow its size_t arithmetic, but every wrapped result converts to a negative int for any table size a font file can carry, and the checks 'tmpnumgattrs < 0 || tmpnumgattrs > 65535' (line 49) reject all such values; no surviving defect.

Lines 69-71 forcibly set _has_boxes = true, overriding the parsed glatflags bit (commented as a compiler workaround). A Glat v3 table whose flags say 'no boxes' will be parsed downstream with box semantics; any memory-safety impact depends on the downstream parser, which is outside this snippet, so it is recorded but not confirmed.

Only the LocaLookup return value size_t(-2) is treated as failure; other error returns (e.g. -1) from the callee would go unchecked, but the callee's error-code contract is not visible in this snippet.
Impact of the version-validation bypass is a fail-open acceptance of out-of-spec tables; whether the downstream legacy-format parser is memory-safe against such data is outside the given code.

verdict.summary: readExtendedClipboard's provide branch allocates per-format buffers inside a loop with no exception guard; if zis.readBytes (or the subsequent length read) throws after earlier buffers were allocated (e.g., a truncated compressed stream), the already-allocated buffers[0..num-1] are never freed because the cleanup loop is skipped when the exception propagates. An attacker can repeatedly send such messages to leak up to maxCutText bytes of heap per message. All other sinks are correctly bounded: allocation sizes are checked against maxCutText before use, indices stay within lengths[16]/buffers[16], and the flags/lengths/buffers bookkeeping (including bit-clearing on rejected formats) keeps the cleanup loop consistent with allocations.

evidence.reason: Root cause: allocations in this loop have no scope guard/try-catch; if zis.readBytes (or a later zis.readU32) throws because the attacker truncated the compressed stream after one or more buffers were successfully allocated, the exception propagates past zis.removeUnderlying() and the delete[] cleanup loop, leaking buffers[0..num-1]. Trigger: send an extended-clipboard provide message whose first format length is <= maxCutText with valid compressed data, followed by a second format whose decompressed data is cut short so readBytes throws mid-read. Repeatable per message for heap exhaustion.

assumptions: ZlibInStream::readBytes/readU32 throw an Exception when the underlying (attacker-supplied) stream is exhausted, as in the TigerVNC rdr implementation; the throw propagates out of this function.
maxCutText is a positive server configuration value bounding per-buffer allocation.
handler is non-NULL per class invariant; handler-side misuse of the passed lengths/buffers is outside this function.
limitations: Caps branch and provide branch index/loop bounds (num ≤ 16) and the 4+4*num length check are all correct; no out-of-bounds access found.

The cleanup loop's use of the mutated flags is consistent with the allocations actually performed (rejected formats clear their bit and do not advance num), so no double-free/use-after-free/ uninitialized-delete exists.

zis.setUnderlying(is, len-4) with len bounded by maxCutText permits CPU/IO decompression amplification via zis.skip of huge rejected lengths, but bytes are discarded, allocations remain bounded by maxCutText, and skip terminates when the stream ends — no memory-safety impact.

If an exception escapes the provide loop, zis.removeUnderlying() is not called explicitly here; in the reference implementation the ZlibInStream destructor performs cleanup, so no stream-state corruption.

verdict.summary: rv10_decode_packet extends the bitreader window with the unvalidated attacker-influenced parameter buf_size2 (s->gb.size_in_bits = 8*buf_size2) without ever checking that buf_size2 does not exceed the buffer extent (buf_size) that init_get_bits registered. A packet with buf_size2 > buf_size and slice data that overruns its declared size causes subsequent ff_h263_decode_mb iterations to read bits beyond the end of buf, a heap out-of-bounds read; the forced ret = SLICE_OK additionally masks the overrun, making the error check at the loop bottom pass against the inflated limit.

evidence.reason: buf_size2 is a packet-derived value crossing the decoder trust boundary and is never validated against buf_size (the extent registered by init_get_bits at line 6). When the first slice's macroblock data runs past buf_size*8 bits and 8*buf_size2 is at least the current bit index, line 79 installs 8*buf_size2 as the new read limit even when buf_size2 > buf_size; the loop's error check (line 82) then evaluates against this inflated limit, so following ff_h263_decode_mb calls read bytes at buf[buf_size..buf_size2-1], past the end of the allocated buffer. Trigger: crafted RV packet with a valid header/mb_count, a slice that overruns its declared size, and buf_size2 > buf_size with 8*buf_size2 >= get_bits_count.

assumptions: buf_size2 originates from container/packet metadata (slice/packet lengths) and is ultimately attacker-controlled; this code contains no check relating it to buf_size or any buffer extent.
get_bits/ff_h263_decode_mb enforce no per-access bounds beyond the caller-side post-hoc size_in_bits comparison performed here.
The decode loop's macroblock-coordinate bounds are correctly guarded by the POS and COUNT checks (lines 15–25), so those sinks are not affected.
limitations: ff_er_add_slice is called with endx = s->mb_x-1, which can be -1 (mb_count == 0, or row wrap before SLICE_END break), and endy can equal mb_height after a full-frame decode; the callee is expected to clip/reject startx > endx and out-of-range end coordinates, but its implementation is not shown, so no memory-safety impact is confirmed here.
8*buf_size2 can overflow int for buf_size2 > 2^28; reaching that requires an implausibly large single packet, so it is not treated as a separate vulnerability.

Stale s->first_slice_line on RV10 resumed mid-frame slices and the forced ret = SLICE_OK masking SLICE_END are decode-robustness/logic issues only; the latter is folded into the confirmed out-of-bounds-read path.
init_get_bits trusting buf_size, and reliance on AV_INPUT_BUFFER_PADDING for reads slightly past buf_size, are caller/API contracts not verifiable from this snippet.

verdict.summary: ff_h264_pred_weight_table trusts the attacker-controlled reference count when expanding weighted-prediction entries for frame pictures. With picture_structure == PICT_FRAME and ref_count > 16, the loop writes past the end of the fixed-size luma_weight table, producing an out-of-bounds write.

evidence.snippet:
pwt->luma_weight[16 + 2 * i][list][0] = pwt->luma_weight[16 + 2 * i + 1][list][0] = pwt->luma_weight[i][list][0];
                pwt->luma_weight[16 + 2 * i][list][1] = pwt->luma_weight[16 + 2 * i + 1][list][1] = pwt->luma_weight[i][list][1];
evidence.reason: The loop bound at line 27 is the attacker-controlled ref_count[list], which is never checked against the table’s 16-entry base capacity. When picture_structure == PICT_FRAME and ref_count[list] >= 17, i reaches 16 and these lines write to pwt->luma_weight[48] and beyond, causing an out-of-bounds write.

assumptions: The H264PredWeightTable arrays are sized for 16 base reference entries, as implied by the 16 + 2*i expansion indexing.
limitations: The exact array dimensions are not shown in the snippet; the analysis relies on the visible indexing scheme to infer the intended capacity.
A separate base-index overflow on pwt->luma_weight[i] would depend on the actual array dimension and is not separately confirmed.

verdict.summary: No reachable security vulnerability found. All indexing into `input` is in-bounds by construction (each index is read only after the previous character matched a non-NUL case); the heap copy in the 'CC <text>' path is safely sized because r_str_unescape and r_str_ansi_strip are strictly shrink-only in-place transformations, so strlen(nc) <= strlen(newcomment) for every input; all heap results (strdup, sdb_decode, r_str_between, r_core_editor) are NULL-checked before use; and the only command string built with interpolated string data (the undo command) is authored and executed solely by the same operator session, crossing no trust boundary, with only a numeric address interpolated into the immediately executed r_core_cmdf call.
